title: I Took the Lighting-Board Checkout to the Intern Who Skipped the Cue Log

parts.text: I stepped into booth one at 5:04 p.m. and intern Sol was already using my numbered showfile. The board said: ONE HOUR. CUES STAY IN THE LOG. I was twenty-six, board op, holding a clipboard that listed our plot. Sol shrugged. "Interns learn the board." I photographed the board, the booking, and his fader on my cue. Then I asked for the cue log. At 5:12 the booth desk pinged why Sol's fader sat on our cue. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The booth desk can see Sol's fader in booth one during our plot.

social.video_title: He skipped the cue log on my numbered showfile — Part 1/2
social.description: Lighting booth, an intern on my cue, a one-hour clock he posted. I logged the fader. Would you have asked for the cue log?

parts.text: Sol called it looks until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the fader still. The showfile went back to my numbered stick. Sol ran a slot of their own and told the next intern atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: INTERNS DO NOT LEARN ON A BOOKED BOARD. I keep our plot on a labeled card. Sol brown-bags his looks. The booth finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Interns do not learn on a booked board — Part 2/2
social.description: Cue log, numbered showfile, and a second line on the board. Were looks ever our plot?
